A1.justification: Both PDFs clearly describe PeKit, and their supplied pages are readable. However, v2 repeatedly refers to an appendix but ends with references on page 11; v3 includes Appendices A–G. This limits comparisons of previously referenced supplementary analyses, while the main-text changes remain assessable.

before.justification: v2 reports original PeKit recognition, captioning and VQA results on MyVLM, Yo’LLaVA and This-Is-My-Img, including component comparisons in Tables 1–3.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and reports additional multi-concept recognition, multi-concept VQA, video QA, ablations and resource measurements.

M1.justification: The feature extraction, memory, retrieval and image-prompting pipeline remains unchanged; multi-object image prompting already existed in v2. Section 3.5 adds a video adaptation that processes sampled frames, maintains consistent object-specific box colors across frames and supplies them to a video LVLM.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained image benchmarks, v3 evaluates simultaneous recognition and open-ended questioning about personalized object pairs, plus video questions requiring temporal understanding. Appendix B describes 11 pairs incorporating additional person concepts and a video QA set. These substantially extend the evaluated task requirements beyond v2’s quantitative single-concept image evaluations.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds unpersonalized LLaVA-OneVision-Qwen2 and InternVideoChat2.5 as comparators for the video experiments. Existing MyVLM, Yo’LLaVA and LLaVA comparisons remain; PeKit with InternVL was already evaluated in v2. This is a focused expansion of the comparator set.

E3.justification: v3 introduces joint-object recognition criteria and GPT-3.5 grading of open-ended multi-concept/video answers, with 55 multi-concept images and 267 video QA pairs. It also revises the reference-view description: v2 ensures the entire object is visible, whereas v3 permits partly visible or otherwise suboptimal views. That is a reported setting revision, without evidence that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 supplies extensive sensitivity analyses for reference-image counts, memory size, retrieval encoders, thresholds and reference vocabulary, plus a video object-naming control and illustrated failure cases. The detector and image-LVLM ablations already present in v2 remain. Some supplementary analyses were referenced in v2’s unavailable appendix, so their inclusion does not establish that they were newly performed.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. v3’s added plots show point estimates without uncertainty bars. The standard deviation used for threshold selection describes reference distances, not uncertainty in experimental performance.

E6.justification: The corresponding original entries in Tables 1–3 are numerically unchanged. New results include multi-concept recognition averaging 72.6% for PeKit versus 54.3% for Yo’LLaVA, and video QA of 35.0% versus the OneVision baseline’s 23.0%, and 61.3% versus InternVideoChat2.5’s 56.6%. These are additional evaluations, accompanied by appendix ablation, resource and qualitative results.

T1.justification: The main formulation and Equations 1–5 are unchanged. Appendix A.4 specifies the threshold rule τi = μi − σi/2 and an adjustable variant, but v2 already refers to automatic object-specific thresholds in its unavailable appendix. Whether this mathematical rule was added or merely disclosed again cannot be determined.

C1.justification: v3 makes multi-concept and video personalization, and their comprehensive evaluation benchmark, central contributions in the abstract, introduction and conclusion. v2 already illustrates multi-concept image capability but frames its performance claims around three image benchmarks. v3 extends those claims to video and joint-object settings and removes the introduction’s privacy-avoidance claim.

C2.justification: Appendix D supplies detailed explanations of noisy-mask failures, small-object feature loss and the potential value of object relationships, with proposed remedies. Appendix A.6 discusses contextual clues leaked by object names. New multi-concept/video interpretations identify reasoning limitations, although the description of joint-object detection as only 'slightly lower' understates the 45.4% versus 83.6% positive-accuracy difference.

D1.justification: v3 provides component sizes, A5000 RTX hardware, module runtime and memory measurements, dataset category/count tables, QA construction procedures and full inference and grading prompts in Appendices A–C. Much of this information was only deferred to an unavailable appendix in v2. These additions substantially improve reproducibility documentation without establishing changes to the retained image experiments.

R1.justification: v3 removes the related-work subsections on LLM personalization, text-to-image personalization and vision foundation models, together with numerous associated citations. It adds Video-ChatGPT and YOLO-World references, drops the explicit 'first training-free' wording and emphasizes scalability beyond prior single-concept/image approaches. This substantially narrows and redirects the research positioning.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, experimental discussion and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Benchmark construction and evaluation metrics receive dedicated subsections, the method summary is removed, related work is condensed, and qualitative comparisons are reorganized into appendices. These are extensive narrative and structural changes beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: Figure 1 rearranges its panels, the benchmark illustration is redesigned to include multi-concept examples, and Tables 2–3 gain separate task blocks. v2 Figure 4 is retained as v3 Figure 12 rather than removed. New qualitative displays, sensitivity plots, failure illustrations and implementation/dataset tables substantially expand the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves the supplied paper by providing supporting analyses and reproducibility details that v2 deferred to an absent appendix, and by directly testing joint-object and video applicability. The failure analyses and naming control make the method’s strengths and limits more assessable. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, notably calling the substantial multi-concept positive-accuracy deficit 'slightly lower'; the retained benchmark scores themselves do not improve.
